concepts.text: Psychology studies mental processes, experiences and behaviour in many contexts
Origin of the word: Greek 'psyche' (soul) and 'logos' (study); shift from study of soul to a science
Levels of analysis: individual, dyad, group and organisation

sections.name: 1.2 What is Psychology? / Psychology as a Discipline

concepts.text: Definition of psychology as the scientific study of mental processes, experiences and behaviour
Mental processes: remembering, learning, knowing, perceiving, feeling, thinking - activities of the mind
Experiences: subjective, embedded in awareness or consciousness; known through the person's report
Behaviour: overt (observable actions) and covert (internal, e.g. heart rate changes) responses to stimuli
Stimulus and response as the basic units of behaviour
Psychology draws on reflection about self and a scientific, objective approach
Roots in philosophy, but modern psychology borrows methods of physics and biology
Hypothetico-deductive model: theory leads to hypotheses tested by experiment
Influence of Descartes and the biological sciences; evolutionary psychology
Importance of objective definitions, measurement and replication
Behaviour studied in its socio-cultural context; humans as social beings
Example-based idea: same event explained through social and cultural factors (e.g. resilience of a poor family)
Psychology as both natural and social science - a bridge discipline
Mind versus brain: mind is not a physical structure but depends on the brain
Mind-body relationship; brain imaging (e.g. fMRI) showing mental activity linked to brain activity
Mind can influence the body: positive visualisation, psychoneuroimmunology example
Behaviour as responses to internal and external stimuli; simple vs complex, short vs enduring

sections.name: 1.6 Popular Notions about the Discipline of Psychology

concepts.text: Everyone acts as a lay psychologist; common-sense explanations of behaviour
Common sense is often hindsight and contradictory (e.g. opposite proverbs)
Scientific psychology tests common-sense ideas systematically; evidence sometimes contradicts them
Examples where research findings contradict popular beliefs about behaviour
Wilhelm Wundt set up the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879
Structuralism (Wundt, Titchener): structure of mind via introspection
Functionalism (William James, John Dewey): what the mind does and how behaviour helps adaptation
Gestalt psychology (Wertheimer, Kohler, Koffka): perception as an organised whole
Behaviourism (John Watson, later Skinner): study only observable behaviour; S-R
Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud): unconscious desires and conflicts
Humanistic perspective (Rogers, Maslow): free will and drive to self-actualise
Cognitive perspective: mind as an information processor; constructivism (Piaget, Vygotsky)
Box: key landmarks in the history of modern psychology (timeline)
Indian philosophical traditions rich in ideas on consciousness, self and mind-body
First psychology laboratory: Calcutta University, 1915 (department 1916) (N.N. Sengupta); first experimental lab
Girindra Shekhar Bose and the Indian Psychoanalytical Association (1922)
Later departments at Mysore, Patna etc.; Durganand Sinha's four phases of growth
Indigenisation and cultural relevance of psychological research in India
Cognitive psychology - attention, memory, perception, problem solving, decision making
Biological psychology and neuropsychology - brain-behaviour links
Developmental psychology - changes across the life span
Social psychology - how others influence our thoughts and behaviour
Cross-cultural and cultural psychology - role of culture in behaviour
Environmental psychology - interaction of physical environment and behaviour
Health psychology - psychological factors in health and illness
Clinical and counselling psychology - causes and treatment of psychological problems
Industrial/organisational psychology - workplace behaviour
Educational and school psychology - learning and school settings
Sports, forensic, military, aviation and space psychology; psycholinguistics; community psychology
Psychology as an interdisciplinary field: links with philosophy, medicine, economics, political science, sociology
Links with computer science (AI), law and criminology, mass communication, music and fine arts, architecture and engineering
Using psychological knowledge to solve personal and social problems
Self-understanding and better decisions, e.g. effective study habits
Contributing to social issues such as health, environment and social justice
Question type: define psychology and explain its subject matter (mind, behaviour, experience)
Question type: compare structuralism, functionalism, behaviourism and other schools
Question type: explain psychology as natural and as social science
Question type: describe branches and match a problem to the right branch
Activity type: compare common-sense beliefs with research evidence
Why psychologists use systematic methods to study behaviour and mental processes
Four goals: description, prediction, explanation, and control / application of behaviour
Description: defining and measuring behaviour precisely
Prediction: forecasting behaviour from known relationships with some accuracy
Explanation: identifying causes (antecedents) of behaviour
Control: making behaviour happen, reduce or increase; application to improve lives
Conceptualising a problem: choosing a topic and forming a testable hypothesis
Collecting data: deciding participants, methods, tools and procedure
Drawing conclusions: statistical analysis and graphical representation of data
Revising research conclusions: confirming or modifying theory; the cyclic nature of research
Positivist / scientific approach versus interpretive approach
Interpretive approach: understanding subjective experiences and meanings in context
Data is not independent of the context: participant characteristics and setting matter
Types of data: demographic information, physical information, physiological data, psychological information
Data not direct measures; inferred from responses
Observation as a systematic, organised and selective process: selection, recording, analysis
Naturalistic versus controlled observation
Non-participant versus participant observation
Strengths and weaknesses: rich data in natural setting vs observer bias and time cost
Experiments establish cause-effect relationships under controlled conditions
Independent and dependent variables; operational definitions
Experimental group and control group
Extraneous / confounding variables and why they must be controlled
Control techniques: elimination, constancy of conditions, counterbalancing, random assignment
Laboratory experiment vs field experiment vs quasi-experiment
Limitations: artificiality, ethical constraints, difficulty controlling all variables
Studying the relationship between two variables to predict one from the other
Correlation coefficient ranges from -1.0 to +1.0
Positive, negative and zero correlation with examples
Correlation does not imply causation
Surveys collect information on opinions, attitudes, and behaviour of a population
Interview: structured / standardised vs unstructured; interviewer and interviewee
Interview formats: individual to individual, individual to group, group to individual, group to group
Questionnaire survey: open-ended vs closed-ended questions (yes/no, multiple choice, rating scale); mailed questionnaires
Telephone survey; advantages and limitations of each survey type
Problems of surveys: social desirability, faking, inaccurate recall
Psychological tests measure individual differences in abilities, aptitude, interests, personality
Standardised test: reliability, validity and norms
Reliability types: test-retest and split-half reliability
Validity: test measures what it claims to measure
Norms and standardised procedure for administration and scoring
Types of tests by language: verbal, non-verbal and performance tests
Types by administration: individual vs group tests; by time: speed vs power tests
In-depth study of a single person or small unit using multiple methods
Use in clinical settings and for rare phenomena; limits on generalisation
Quantitative method: numerical data, statistical analysis
Qualitative method: narratives, descriptions, interviews; analysis of meaning
Using both methods together (triangulation) for fuller understanding
Lack of a true zero point in psychological measurement
Relative nature of psychological tools - need cultural adaptation
Subjective interpretation of qualitative data
Voluntary participation of research participants
Informed consent before the study
Debriefing after the study to remove any anxiety
Sharing the results of the study with participants
Confidentiality of data and privacy of participants

Question type: choose the appropriate method for a given research question
Question type: interpret correlation values and direction
Question type: list ethical guidelines for a given study

Development: pattern of progressive, orderly and predictable changes
Growth (increase in size) vs maturation (changes following a genetic plan) vs development
Development involves biological, cognitive and socio-emotional processes, which interact
Development is lifelong; no age dominates
Development is multi-dimensional and multi-directional (gains and losses)
Development is highly plastic
Development is influenced by historical conditions
Development is studied by many disciplines and is contextual (heredity-environment interplay)

Environment: physical and social surroundings; nature-nurture interaction
Genes set a reaction range; environment determines where in that range a person ends up
Some traits are strongly shaped by genes, others more open to environmental influence

Culture shapes developmental goals and parenting
Developmental stages and the idea of developmental tasks expected at each stage

Sensory abilities of newborns: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch
Piaget's sensorimotor stage: learning through senses and actions; object permanence

Physical development: slower growth, gross and fine motor skills, handedness
Piaget's preoperational stage: symbolic thought, pretend play, egocentrism, animism

Socio-emotional development: self-concept, gender roles, self-esteem
Erikson's stages of autonomy vs shame/doubt, initiative vs guilt, industry vs inferiority
Kohlberg's moral development: preconventional, conventional and postconventional levels
Parenting and peer influence on child's development
Adolescence as transition from childhood to adulthood (about 12 to 18-20 years)
Physical changes of puberty: growth spurt, menarche, secondary sex characteristics; early vs late maturation
Cognitive development: formal operational thought, abstract and hypothetical-deductive reasoning, idealism
Adolescent egocentrism: imaginary audience and personal fable
Moral reasoning in adolescence; questioning values
Forming an identity: Erikson's identity vs role confusion; role of family, peers, culture, vocation
Major concerns: delinquency, substance abuse and eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia)

Early adulthood tasks: career and work, marriage, parenthood, intimacy vs isolation

We know the world through sensation, attention and perception working together
Sensation: detecting stimuli by sense organs; perception: interpreting them
Stimuli vary in type (light, sound, smell, taste, touch) and in intensity and other features
Receptors / sense organs specialised for specific stimuli
Seven senses: five external (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin) and two internal (kinesthetic, vestibular)
Kinesthetic sense: position of body parts; vestibular sense: balance and gravity
Functional limitations of sense organs: absolute threshold
Difference threshold / just noticeable difference (JND)
Psychophysics as the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and sensations
Attention: selecting some stimuli out of many; arousal, alertness and concentration
Focus (centre) and fringe (margin) of attention
Types of attention: selective, sustained, divided; span of attention
External factors: size, intensity, motion, novelty, colour, complexity of stimuli
Internal factors: motivational (needs) and cognitive (interest, attitude, preparatory set)
Filter theory (Broadbent): one stimulus allowed through a selective filter to STM
Filter-attenuation theory (Treisman): unattended input weakened, not blocked
Multimode theory (Johnston and Heinz): selection can occur at different stages
Sustained attention / vigilance: concentrating for long periods (e.g. radar operator)
Factors: sensory modality, clarity of stimuli, temporal uncertainty, spatial uncertainty
Box: Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) - inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity
Perception as giving meaning to sensory input; recognising objects
Bottom-up processing: from parts to whole
Top-down processing: from whole and expectations to parts
Perceiver's motivation and needs affect perception (e.g. hungry person sees food)
Expectations / perceptual set
Cognitive styles: field-dependent vs field-independent
Socio-cultural background and experiences
Gestalt idea: the whole is more than the sum of parts; we perceive organised wholes (form)
Figure-ground segregation and reversible figures
Principles: proximity, similarity, continuity, smallness, symmetry, surroundedness, closure

sections.name: 4.8 Perception of Space, Depth and Distance

concepts.text: Converting 2-D retinal images into 3-D perception
Monocular cues (psychological cues): relative size, interposition/overlap, linear perspective
Monocular cues: aerial perspective, light and shade, relative height, texture gradient, motion parallax
Binocular cues: retinal disparity, convergence, accommodation
Size constancy
Shape constancy
Brightness constancy
Illusions as misperceptions of real stimuli shared by most people
Geometrical illusion: Muller-Lyer illusion
Apparent movement illusion: phi phenomenon (as in films)

Carpentered-world idea and differences across cultural groups
Indian research on depth perception in pictures and cultural factors

Learning as a key process by which behaviour changes through experience
Definition: relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience or practice
Changes due to maturation, fatigue, drugs or injury are not learning
Features: always involves experience, changes are relatively permanent, learning is inferred from performance
Learning as a process with sequence of psychological events (pre-test, practice, post-test)
Overview of learning types: classical and operant conditioning, observational, cognitive, verbal, skill learning
Simplest form - associative learning; conditioning
Pavlov's experiment with dogs: salivation to bell paired with food
Unconditioned stimulus (US) and unconditioned response (UR)
Conditioned stimulus (CS) and conditioned response (CR)
Acquisition through repeated CS-US pairing; everyday examples (fear, liking)

Type of unconditioned stimulus: appetitive vs aversive
Intensity of the conditioned stimulus
B.F. Skinner: operants are voluntary behaviours controlled by consequences
Skinner box experiment with rats pressing lever
Instrumental: the response is instrumental in getting the reward
Reinforcer types: positive and negative reinforcers
Primary vs secondary reinforcers
Number, amount and quality of reinforcement
Schedules of reinforcement: continuous vs partial
Partial schedules: fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval
Delayed reinforcement weakens learning
Punishment vs negative reinforcement
Escape and avoidance conditioning
Reinforcement and its role in strengthening responses
Extinction: response weakens when reinforcement stops
Spontaneous recovery after extinction
Generalisation: responding to similar stimuli
Discrimination: responding differently to different stimuli
Shaping and chaining through successive approximations
Learning by observing others (modelling, social learning)
Bandura's Bobo doll experiment with children - observed aggression rewarded/punished
Observational learning in socialisation, fashion and social skills
Learning involving changes in knowledge, not just behaviour
Insight learning (Kohler's chimpanzee Sultan): sudden solution, transfer to new problems
Latent learning (Tolman): learning without reinforcement; cognitive map
Learning words and verbal material; Ebbinghaus nonsense syllables
Methods: paired-associates learning (stimulus and response terms)
Serial learning (learning in order)
Free recall (any order)
Determinants: list length, meaningfulness, frequency; organisation - clustering and subjective organisation
Nature of skills: complex sequences of perceptual-motor responses (driving, typing)
Phases of skill acquisition (Fitts): cognitive, associative, autonomous
Role of practice and feedback in skill learning
Continuous vs partial reinforcement and resistance to extinction
Motivation: intrinsic and extrinsic
Preparedness for learning: species-specific biological readiness
Learning disability: difficulties in reading, writing, speaking, reasoning or maths despite normal intelligence
Symptoms: letter/word reversals (e.g. b/d), poor spelling, attention and memory problems, motor clumsiness, poor time and space sense
Dyslexia and related disorders; not due to intellectual disability
Remedial teaching and early identification

Memory: retaining and recovering information over time
Three stages: encoding, storage and retrieval

sections.name: 6.3 Information Processing Approach: The Stage Model

concepts.text: Computer analogy of memory
Atkinson-Shiffrin stage model (1968): sensory memory, short-term memory, long-term memory
Control processes: attention, rehearsal move information between stores

sections.name: 6.4 Memory Systems: Sensory, Short-term and Long-term Memories

concepts.text: Sensory memory: large capacity, very brief (under a second); iconic (visual) and echoic (auditory)
Short-term memory: about 7 plus or minus 2 items, about 18-30 seconds; acoustic encoding
Maintenance rehearsal keeps items in STM; chunking increases capacity
Long-term memory: unlimited capacity, semantic encoding, long duration
Forgetting from STM by decay and interference; Peterson and Peterson style experiment
Working memory (Baddeley): phonological loop, visuo-spatial sketchpad, central executive
Criticisms of the stage model and reasons for alternative models
Craik and Lockhart (1972): memory depends on depth of processing
Structural (physical) processing - shallow
Phonetic (sound) processing - intermediate
Semantic (meaning) processing - deep, best retention
Elaborative rehearsal vs maintenance rehearsal
Declarative (explicit) memory: facts, names, dates; can be verbalised
Procedural (non-declarative) memory: how to do things, skills; hard to verbalise
Episodic memory (Tulving): personal life events with time and place
Semantic memory: general knowledge, concepts, language rules
Implicit memories: memories not consciously recalled (e.g. priming)
Ebbinghaus: nonsense syllables, savings method, forgetting curve - rapid early loss then levelling off
Forgetting due to trace decay (disuse); limitations of this explanation
Interference: proactive interference (old blocks new)
Retroactive interference (new blocks old)
Retrieval failure: cues not available (Tulving); tip-of-tongue type cases
Motivated forgetting / repression
Mnemonics using images: keyword method (foreign language words)
Method of loci: placing items at familiar locations
Mnemonics using organisation: chunking
First-letter technique (acronyms, e.g. VIBGYOR)
General tips: deep processing, minimising interference, giving retrieval cues, PQRST-style active study
